This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. 1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. If the gripping surfaces of each part are driven separately, the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive is given up: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. If the split body is instead pulled closed on the pipe, the closing force passes through the joint at the split and the pipe itself reacts the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe, and a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is needed, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. An added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, that plane passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame, its segments being in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
22	
23	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch 16 acts through a wedge 52 as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge 52 can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
24	
25	The jaw carriages
26	
27	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.
28	
29	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
30	
31	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
32	
33	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
34	
35	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
36	
37	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
38	
39	The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52, the wedge 52 being movable by the latch 16. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
40	
41	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the first cam ring segment 22, the second cam ring segment 24 and the ring drive face 36.
42	
43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
44	
45	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
46	
47	The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
52	
53	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
54	
55	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.
58

The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The present disclosure relates to clamps that grip the outside of a pipe, and more particularly to a reusable split clamp whose frame opens on a hinge so that the clamp can be placed around a pipe from the side, and whose radially movable jaws are advanced together onto the pipe by a single latch motion.

==> /home/nimrod_rotem/patent-search-pilot/data/draft_workspaces/p9/draft/06-summary.md <==
A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

input.summary: Corrective QA pass only. The reviewer raised one item: the FIG. 1 brief stated the three jaw carriages' circumferential positions and their allocation between the two frame halves as fact, although the disclosure says only that the carriages are "distributed around the closed frame", and the identical choice is expressly marked schematic in the FIG. 2 brief. I added the schematic qualifier to that one sentence in figures/FIG-1.md and changed nothing else. I did not adopt the reviewer's suggested cross-reference to "the three oblique slots 34 in FIG. 2", because naming that part and its numeral inside the FIG. 1 brief would put a part in a brief whose reference-numeral list does not carry it, which is itself a defect; the schematic qualifier alone is what the finding requires, and FIG. 2 already carries the matching qualifier for the slot positions, so the two briefs now label the choice the same way. No application text, no claim, and no numeral changed, so the numeral table, the Brief Description and the Detailed Description remain in step. I re-checked the rest of the draft against the disclosure: claims 1-15, all 26 numerals, the six figure briefs, the abstract at 142 words, the "Not applicable" cross-reference and government-support statements, and the absence of any placeholder, drafting note, editorial aside or em dash. Per the drafting brief, note plainly that no prior-art search was run for this application: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background contains no citations and the art you have been given may be incomplete. A later search could surface references that bear on the claims as written.
reasoning: The reviewer's finding is a real depiction-convention defect, not a false positive. A plan view has to put three carriages somewhere, so the positions are a drawing necessity, but one-on-the-first-half and two-on-the-second-half is also a count-per-part assertion, and it happens to place two carriages on the segment the wedge drives directly. The disclosure never allocates them. Marking the whole placement schematic keeps the drawing honest without importing the allocation into the invention.

I confined the fix to the figure brief. The claims and description are already position-neutral: claim 9 recites only that the three jaw carriages are distributed around the frame such that they approach the pipe from three different directions, and the description says the same. Adding anything to the text to justify a drawing choice would have run the invention off the source, and the drawing is never authority for the text.

I departed from the reviewer's suggested wording in one respect. The suggestion appended 'chosen to correspond to the positions of the three oblique slots 34 in FIG. 2'. Numeral 34 is not on the FIG. 1 sheet and the oblique slots are not visible in that view, so importing the canonical part name and numeral into the FIG. 1 brief would create a numeral-list mismatch of exactly the kind the numeral check catches. The qualifier by itself satisfies the finding.

Claim 1 rests on the coupling relationship the disclosure calls essential: complementary coupling faces at both the hinge end and the latch end that are engaged by the closing motion itself, so the two cam ring segments rotate as one coupled ring, combined with a wedge driven by the latch against a ring drive face and a force-limiting spring stack in the drive train between latch handle and wedge that absorbs post-contact handle travel instead of driving one carriage deeper. That combination is what carries the claim; with no references in prior_art/, there was nothing to write around beyond keeping the claim tied to the disclosed relationship.

Left out of claim 1 deliberately and kept as dependent fallbacks: the indicator pin and its predetermined compression range (claims 2, 3, 11, 14), the two-position over-center latch (claims 4, 12), the diameter-independent seating of the pivoting pads (claim 5), the mounting boss and the equipment it carries (claims 8, 10), and the semicircular halves with the three-direction approach (claim 9). Each of those is separately arguable, so none of them needs to sit in the broadest claim.

I verified the internal chains the previous review had already closed rather than reworking them: section line 3-3 appears identically in the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 3 brief, the Brief Description and the Detailed Description and is excluded from the numeral table; every numeral in a brief appears once in draft/numerals.md against one part name; each sheet lists eight numerals or fewer.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat cut into the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc running downward from the right joint. Its upper end, the end nearer that joint, lies radially inside the outer boundary and stops below the joint, so a short piece of the circular outer boundary runs on from it to the joint. Its lower end, further from the joint, meets the circular outer boundary. Between the two ends the flat is one straight edge, so the material cut from the segment is deepest at the upper end and runs out to nothing at the lower end. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.

- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length, form and slant of the ring drive face 36, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the slant of its lower face, the attitude, outline and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the stack drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so it descends from left to right toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position, as a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which it is read.

- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown, the frame and the two cam ring segments being shown in section at the break. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut material carries section hatching; the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each of the two cam ring segments carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches, so the parting line and the contact between the segment end faces stay distinct. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at each body's radially outer side.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, filling the upper and lower parts of the view, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

input.summary: All seven findings were in figures/ briefs, and all seven are fixed. Each fix removes a statement of functional-surface geometry that the disclosure does not make, and leaves in its place the minimally specific generic face, slot, joint, or fit that still shows the disclosed function, so no drawing loses a disclosed part and no numeral or application sentence had to move. FIG. 2: the ring drive face is now a short straight flat on the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment near the right joint, at an inclination such that an advancing wedge moves the ring circumferentially, with the deeper end, runout direction, and end positions relative to the joint deleted; and the oblique slots now recite only that all three are alike and tilt the same way so one direction of ring rotation moves all three followers inwardly, with the counterclockwise handedness deleted and the sense of tilt marked schematic. FIG. 4: the same drive face is now one straight surface at an inclination to the radially outer side of the band with length, slant, and end positions marked schematic; the wedge now bears on that face with its lower face inclined so advance moves the band circumferentially, with matched slant, full-length contact, and the named drive direction deleted; and the asserted structural interruption of the frame wall is replaced by an opening over the short region where the wedge meets the drive face, with the extent marked schematic, matched in the header schematic list. FIG. 6: the frame wall interruption is replaced by a band of hatched frame material between the channel and the break line, so the lower body now reads like the upper body, and the latch-end coupling joint now recites only that the two end faces lie against one another where they meet so one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other, with the form and extent of engagement marked schematic. FIG. 3 and FIG. 5: the running-clearance fit at the annular-guide walls is replaced in both by a block received between the groove walls, held against radial movement and free to move circumferentially, with the fit marked schematic, which is the same relationship the detailed description already states. The reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, and claims are unchanged and remain synchronized: every numeral listed on each sheet is still shown on it, numeral targets still land on parts that still exist in the briefs, and FIG. 6 no longer refers to FIG. 4 for a feature neither view now asserts. No note, placeholder, question, or instruction to a person appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/.
reasoning: The findings all share one root: the briefs described a cam ramp, a cam slot, a coupling joint, and a guide fit at a level of detail an engineer would choose when designing the part, not at the level the inventor disclosed. The disclosure says the latch drives a wedge against a drive face and rotates the ring, and that oblique slots convert that rotation into synchronized inward travel. It never says which end of the ramp is deeper, which way the cut runs out, which way the ring turns, how far the wedge bears, or how the coupling faces meet. I removed each such statement and kept only the function it was there to show.

For every removal I kept a positive geometric statement, because a renderer still has to draw something: an inclined flat on the outer boundary rather than a tapered ramp with a named deep end; three like slots tilted the same way rather than slots with a named handedness; end faces lying against one another rather than a full-width butt contact; a block received between the groove walls rather than a stated running clearance. Nothing was replaced with a negative instruction about linework.

The frame-wall finding mattered most because it cut against the application text. The detailed description says the annular guide holds the ring against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially, and the briefs were asserting an arc where the outer guide wall was missing and the ring exposed. The correct direction of repair was to change the drawing to match the text, not the text to match the drawing, so FIG. 4 now shows only an opening where the wedge reaches the disclosed drive face and FIG. 6 shows continuous frame material on both sides of the joint.

Removing the drive-face taper and the slot handedness also removed the pair of assertions that previously fixed the clamping rotation direction between FIG. 2 and FIG. 4. That is the intended outcome, since the disclosure never names a rotation sense. The two briefs stay consistent with each other because neither now names one, and each expressly marks the sense as schematic.

The FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 fits were given identical wording deliberately. Both sheets section the same annular guide with the same ring in it, so a single phrasing keeps the two views from implying two different retention schemes, and the phrasing was taken from the relationship the detailed description already states rather than from a fit class.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle, with a short block reaching to it from each frame end, the whole hinge 14 lying within the width of the frame body.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with a lever reaching radially outward from it, inclined toward the first frame half 10, the over-center attitude.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, the topmost on the first frame half 10 and the others on the second frame half 12, these three circumferential positions and their distribution between the two frame halves being shown schematically. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the jaw carriage 30 is shown schematically as a block reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the topmost carriage block.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, so that one direction of rotation of the ring moves all three followers inwardly; the sense of the tilt is shown schematically and is not otherwise specified.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat on the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc near the right joint, lying at an inclination to the circular outer boundary so that a wedge advancing on it can move the ring circumferentially. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the frame body, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriage 30 with its follower 32, and the jaw pad 40 each carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block is received in the groove between its walls above and below, held against radial movement and free to move circumferentially, the fit shown schematically. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular opening passes through that block from its left face to its right face; apart from that opening the block is solid and hatched throughout. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the opening, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel holding the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the extent of the opening in the frame wall at the wedge, the length, form and slant of the ring drive face 36, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the slant of its lower face, the attitude, outline and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the stack drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

Between the latch housing 58 and the left band the frame wall is open over the short region in which the wedge 52 meets the ring drive face 36, the extent of that opening being shown schematically. In that region the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface lying at an inclination to the radially outer side of the band, its length, slant and end positions shown schematically.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity, its lower face inclined to bear on the ring drive face 36, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the band circumferentially. The direction of advance, the slant of the lower face and the extent of the bearing are shown schematically.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position, as a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which it is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. Each body ends at the parting line in a straight end face, and the channel that holds its band opens at that end face, so the end region of each band is exposed at the parting line.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and meets the ring drive face 36 in a plain inclined contact, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the band circumferentially. The form and extent of that contact and the direction of advance are shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs from the wedge 52 upward toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, drawn to show it lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall of the housing and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58, that outer surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

input.summary: Five findings, all in figures/, all fixed; the claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions and draft/numerals.md are untouched and remain synchronized with the briefs. FIG. 4 no longer asserts any opening, window or break in the frame wall: the cavity of the latch housing 58 now opens downward toward the parting line between the two frame end faces, where the channel holding each band opens at the end face so the end region of each band is exposed, which is the same guide-opening arrangement FIG. 6 already describes, and the wedge 52 meets the ring drive face 36 there. The ring drive face is no longer given a radial side, an owning segment, or a wedge approach direction: in FIG. 2 it is now a short plain straight face of the segmented cam ring 20 in the region of the right joint, drawn inclined so a wedge bearing on it can move the ring circumferentially, with the carrying segment, radial side, slant and extent expressly not specified; in FIG. 4 the wedge meets it in a plain inclined contact so that advance of the wedge moves the band circumferentially, with the form and extent of the contact and the direction of advance marked schematic, and the header schematic list rewritten to match. The undisclosed handle mounting is gone: the latch handle 50 is now a plain straight bar of even width standing above the latch housing 58, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright in the over-center position, with its mounting not depicted, no pivot joint and no opening between the housing walls; the spring stack line, which formerly ran to the handle pivot, now runs from the wedge 52 upward toward the latch handle 50 in the cavity so it still reads as lying in the drive train between handle and wedge, and the indicator pin 56 now simply rises from the stack and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge it is read against. FIG. 3 no longer states that the oblique slot breaks out: the opening is now formed in the left face of the cam ring block, sized to receive the follower 32, and is not shown breaking out at the right face; its numeral target is now the open space of the opening beside the post, which no longer implies a depth. FIG. 1 keeps only the small circle on the left joint line for the hinge 14, with the knuckle blocks reaching from each frame end and the containment of the hinge within the frame width deleted. Every numeral listed on each sheet is still shown on that sheet, and every numeral target still lands on a body the brief still describes.
reasoning: The frame-wall opening and the handle pivot were the same kind of defect: the brief had solved an engineering problem the inventor left open, then labelled the solution schematic. A hole through a load-bearing wall and a joint at a named location are structure and force path, so I removed both rather than re-labelling them.

For the wedge access I took the route that costs nothing structurally: FIG. 6 already shows each frame half's annular guide opening at the end face toward the parting line, so the ring end regions are exposed there without any new aperture. Putting the housing cavity over that parting line lets the wedge reach the drive face using only geometry another sheet already carries, which also keeps the two latch-end views consistent with each other.

On the drive face I kept exactly the generic fact the description carries, that the face is inclined so wedge advance turns the ring, and pushed everything else into an express non-specification. The drawing still has to put the face somewhere, so FIG. 4 draws it at the exposed band end region at the left of the parting line while stating that the carrying segment, radial side, slant and extent are not specified; that keeps the sheet renderable without letting the picture decide which segment carries the face.

Removing the handle pivot broke two dependent statements, so I repaired them instead of leaving dangling references: the spring stack line no longer terminates at a pivot that no longer exists, and the indicator pin no longer needs a stated hole in the top wall to be read against the fixed edge. Both now say only what the disclosure supports, that the stack lies between handle and wedge and that the pin is read against a fixed edge of the housing.

The slot fix matters beyond the drawing because a slot that breaks out at the far face is a different part from a slot that receives a follower. The disclosure says only received in, so FIG. 3 now shows a blind opening in the near face sized to the follower, and I changed the numeral target from right of the post to beside the post so the leader no longer points at an implied through-depth.

No application text moved, and none needed to: claim 1 and the detailed description already speak of a follower received in an oblique slot, a wedge bearing on a ring drive face, and a force-limiting spring stack in the drive train between latch handle and wedge, without ever fixing the slot depth, the radial side of the face, or how the handle is hung. That is why every fix could be confined to figures/.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so no citation appears in the Background and none was added this turn. The independent claims continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge takes up the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: splitting the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn removed only drawing-level detail about a wall opening, a ramp's radial side, a handle mounting, a slot's breakout and hinge knuckles, none of which appears in any claim, so claim scope is unchanged. Since the drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.
input.answer: Every listed mechanical check and reviewer finding is now addressed, and all changes are confined to figures/. The two critical items: FIG. 4 no longer describes any opening, window or break in the frame wall, and instead reaches the drive face the way FIG. 6 already shows the guide arranged, with each band channel opening at the frame end face so the band end regions are exposed at the parting line and the latch housing cavity opening downward over them; and the ring drive face is now described in both FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 as a short plain straight inclined face on which a wedge bears to move the ring circumferentially, with the carrying segment, the radial side, the slant, the extent and the direction of wedge advance expressly not specified. The major item: the latch handle is now a plain straight bar standing above the housing and leaning past upright in the over-center position, with its mounting not depicted and no pivot joint or opening between the housing walls; the spring stack line and the indicator pin were rewritten so neither depends on the deleted pivot or on a stated hole in the housing wall. The two minor items: the oblique slot in FIG. 3 is now an opening in the near face of the cam ring block sized to receive the follower and is not shown breaking out at the far face, with its leader retargeted to the open space beside the post, and the FIG. 1 hinge is now just the small circle on the left joint line, without knuckle blocks or the containment statement. The claims, the detailed description, the drawing descriptions and the numeral table were not changed, since none of them recited any of the removed geometry, and each sheet still shows every numeral listed for it with every leader landing on a body the brief still describes.

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form, slant and extent of the ring drive face 36 and which part of the ring carries it; the form and extent of its contact with the wedge 52 and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face, so each band end region is exposed at the parting line.

There the exposed end region of the left band presents the ring drive face 36, a short plain straight face drawn inclined so that a wedge bearing on it can move the ring circumferentially; which segment carries it, its radial side, slant and extent are not specified.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the exposed band end regions. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and meets the ring drive face 36 in a plain inclined contact, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the band circumferentially.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Nothing was removed from the drawing: all eight numerals (22, 24, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58) are still listed and each is still introduced by name in the prose, and every disclosed relationship the sheet carries survives, namely the two frame bodies each holding an arcuate cam ring segment, the parting line where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces with each band's channel opening at its body's end face so the end region is exposed, the ring drive face at that exposed end region drawn inclined so a wedge bearing on it moves the ring circumferentially, the latch housing cavity opening downward over the exposed band end regions with the wedge in it meeting that face in a plain inclined contact, the force-limiting spring stack lying in the drive train between the latch handle and the wedge, the handle standing above the housing and leaning past upright in the over-center position with its mounting not depicted, and the indicator pin projecting beyond the top wall outer surface that serves as the fixed edge. The savings came from wording rather than content: the schematic list was punctuated into clauses instead of repeated phrases, the two sentences that restated the contact form, contact extent, and direction of wedge advance were dropped because the schematic list already carries all three, and duplicated references such as the top wall of the latch housing 58 and the exposed end regions of the two bands were shortened where the antecedent was already fixed in the same paragraph. No claim, no sentence of the detailed description, no drawing description, and no entry in draft/numerals.md was touched, and the other five briefs are unchanged and were not flagged. The reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims, and all six figure files remain synchronized.
reasoning: The overrun was concentrated in two places, so that is where I cut. The schematic-convention list had grown by accretion as earlier findings were fixed, each one appending a full clause, and the wedge paragraph then repeated the same three conventions in prose. Stating them once in the list and letting the prose describe only the physical contact removed about a third of the excess without weakening the source-fidelity hedges that earlier reviews required.

I protected the hedges deliberately. The clauses saying that the carrying segment, radial side, slant and extent of the ring drive face are not specified, and that the handle mounting is not depicted, are what keep this sheet from re-asserting the untraced geometry that was removed in earlier passes, so they stayed intact even though they cost characters.

The rest of the reduction is redundancy, not substance: second and third mentions of the latch housing and of the band end regions were shortened to the top wall and the exposed band end regions once their antecedents were fixed in the same paragraph, and the parting-line sentence was merged with the sentence identifying which band is which segment.

I did not touch the numeral list, even though it is not counted toward the limit, because trimming the FIG. 36 target would have made the leader endpoint less able to distinguish the drive face from the coupling surfaces meeting at the same parting line.

No other brief needed work: the gate measured only FIG. 4 over the limit, and no finding in this report reached the application text, so the claims, description, drawing descriptions and numeral table stay exactly as they were.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor identifies as essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn changed only the length of one figure brief, so claim scope is untouched. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.
