23	
24	- **[critical] Description asserts an undisclosed inclination of the ring drive face 36 relative to the wedge's direction of advance** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, "The segmented cam ring" section, paragraph beginning "The segmented cam ring 20 furth) - The application text gives the ring drive face 36 a specific angular relationship to the wedge's travel. The inventor passage discloses only that the wedge is driven against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the ring; it says nothing about the face's angle, slant, or orientation relative to the wedge's advance. The inclination is not entailed: a wedge can rotate the ring by acting through its own inclined face against a circumferentially facing ring face, so making the ring's face inclined is an added, unsupported geometry choice. # FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it and where the ring drive face 36 is formed.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, so that one direction of rotation of the ring moves all three followers inwardly; the sense of the tilt is shown schematically and is not otherwise specified.

The ring drive face 36 is a short plain straight face formed in the face of the annulus near the latch end of the ring and spaced circumferentially from the right joint, drawn inclined so that a wedge bearing on it can move the ring circumferentially; which segment carries it, its slant and its extent are not specified; it is drawn within the width of the annulus, and both circular boundaries of the annulus run unbroken.

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. # FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form, slant and extent of the ring drive face 36 and its carrier; the form and extent of its contact with the wedge 52 and the wedge's direction of advance; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

One of the two bands presents the ring drive face 36 in its face at a position spaced circumferentially from the parting line, a short plain straight face drawn inclined so that a wedge bearing on it can move the ring circumferentially; which segment carries it, its slant and its extent are not specified.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and meets the ring drive face 36 in a plain inclined contact, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the band circumferentially.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

content.content: 43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. That advance of the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36 moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, and the positions and tilt of the three slots.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, so that one direction of rotation of the ring moves all three followers inwardly; the sense of the tilt is shown schematically and is not otherwise specified.

The ring drive face 36 is a short plain face at the latch end of the ring, presented at the outer boundary of the annulus so that a wedge acting from outside the ring can bear on it; which segment carries it, and its position, form, extent and depth, are not specified and are shown schematically.

content.text: All three findings are fixed: the FIG. 5 boss relationship, the FIG. 2 drive-face location, and the wedge's inclined face in the description.

input.summary: Three findings, all fixed. FIG. 5 no longer verbalizes a structural relationship between the mounting boss and the guide wall: the block now projects from the outer surface of the body, is joined to it along its base, stands outside the groove with no part reaching into it, and is drawn schematically as a plain rectangular block whose placement relative to the groove is likewise schematic. The statements that it stood radially outside the groove and that the radially outer wall of the groove lay between its base and the groove are gone, which brings the brief into line with the description, which says only that the boss stands outside the annular guide 18 with no part reaching into it. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 now place ring drive face 36 in one location: FIG. 2 presents the face at the outer boundary of the annulus at the latch end so that a wedge acting from outside the ring can bear on it, with the carrying segment and the position, form, extent and depth unspecified and schematic; the sentence confining the face within the annulus width with both circular boundaries unbroken is deleted; and the flat-face sentence again excepts only the three slots. That matches the layout FIG. 4 already commits to, where the housing cavity is open toward the band carrying the face and the wedge bears on it, so numeral 36 leads to one surface in both views. The FIG. 2 leader for 36 now targets the short plain face at the outer boundary near the right joint, and because that put two leaders on the same circle, the segmented cam ring leader moved to the outer boundary in the upper left, clear of the drive face and of both joints. In the detailed description the wedge no longer has an inclined face: it is now positioned to bear on the ring drive face 36, and the advance of the wedge against that face moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially so the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke. That restores agreement with claim 1, which recites only a wedge positioned to bear on a ring drive face, and with FIG. 4, which draws the wedge as a plain block. Nothing else changed: the claims, the Summary, the Abstract, draft/07-drawings.md and draft/numerals.md are untouched, every numeral listed for a sheet is still named on it, and all six briefs remain within the length limit, FIG. 2 at about 2050 characters and FIG. 5 at about 1810.
reasoning: The FIG. 5 sentence had turned a placement into a topology. Saying the outer wall of the groove lies between the boss base and the groove tells a reader how the boss is mounted relative to the guide, which the disclosure never does; it says only that the boss is outside the annular guide. The brief now states the two facts that are disclosed, joined to the body and clear of the groove, and marks the rest as depiction.

For the drive face I aligned FIG. 2 to FIG. 4 rather than the reverse, because FIG. 4 is the view that has to show the wedge reaching the face, and the housing, cavity and wedge in that view are all disclosed parts whose arrangement was already settled. Moving FIG. 2's face to the outer boundary was the smaller change and it leaves one surface for numeral 36 in both sheets.

Deleting the within-the-annulus-width sentence was the necessary half of that fix. A face confined to the axial flat with both circular boundaries unbroken is unreachable by a wedge coming from outside the ring, so leaving that sentence in place would have preserved the very incompatibility the finding names.

Retargeting the drive-face leader forced a second look at the cam ring leader, since both would then have landed on the outer boundary near the right of the view. Moving the ring leader to the upper left keeps it clear of the drive face at the latch end and of the coupling faces at both joints, so each of the three leaders on that circle resolves to a different feature.

Removing the wedge's inclined face cost nothing and fixed a three-way disagreement: the claims already said only that the wedge bears on the ring drive face, FIG. 4 draws a plain block and leaves the contact schematic, and only the description asserted which face of the wedge made contact. I also dropped the repetition that the replacement introduced, so the sentence reads as one statement rather than naming the face twice.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn removed an undisclosed boss-to-guide relationship from one brief, harmonized where the drive face is drawn, and deleted the wedge's inclined face from the description; none of these appears in any claim, so claim scope is unchanged. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.
input.answer: All three findings are fixed. FIG. 5 now says only that the block projects from the outer surface of the body, is joined along its base, and stands outside the groove with no part reaching into it, with its placement relative to the groove shown schematically, so the brief no longer asserts that the guide's outer wall lies between the boss base and the groove; that matches the description, which recites only that the boss stands outside the annular guide. FIG. 2 now presents ring drive face 36 as a short plain face at the latch end at the outer boundary of the annulus, so that a wedge acting from outside the ring can bear on it, with the carrying segment and its position, form, extent and depth unspecified and schematic; the sentence confining the face within the annulus width is deleted and the flat-face sentence again excepts only the three slots, so FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 now put numeral 36 on the same surface. The statements that it stood radially outside the groove and that the radially outer wall of the groove lay between its base and the groove are gone, which brings the brief into line with the description, which says only that the boss stands outside the annular guide 18 with no part reaching into it. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 now place ring drive face 36 in one location: FIG. 2 presents the face at the outer boundary of the annulus at the latch end so that a wedge acting from outside the ring can bear on it, with the carrying segment and the position, form, extent and depth unspecified and schematic; the sentence confining the face within the annulus width with both circular boundaries unbroken is deleted; and the flat-face sentence again excepts only the three slots. That matches the layout FIG. 4 already commits to, where the housing cavity is open toward the band carrying the face and the wedge bears on it, so numeral 36 leads to one surface in both views. The FIG. 2 leader for 36 now targets the short plain face at the outer boundary near the right joint, and because that put two leaders on the same circle, the segmented cam ring leader moved to the outer boundary in the upper left, clear of the drive face and of both joints. In the detailed description the wedge no longer has an inclined face: it is now positioned to bear on the ring drive face 36, and the advance of the wedge against that face moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially so the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke. That restores agreement with claim 1, which recites only a wedge positioned to bear on a ring drive face, and with FIG. 4, which draws the wedge as a plain block. reasoning: The FIG. 5 sentence had turned a placement into a topology. Saying the outer wall of the groove lies between the boss base and the groove tells a reader how the boss is mounted relative to the guide, which the disclosure never does; it says only that the boss is outside the annular guide. The brief now states the two facts that are disclosed, joined to the body and clear of the groove, and marks the rest as depiction.

Moving FIG. 2's face to the outer boundary was the smaller change and it leaves one surface for numeral 36 in both sheets.

A face confined to the axial flat with both circular boundaries unbroken is unreachable by a wedge coming from outside the ring, so leaving that sentence in place would have preserved the very incompatibility the finding names.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, and the positions and tilt of the three slots.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, so that one direction of rotation of the ring moves all three followers inwardly; the sense of the tilt is shown schematically and is not otherwise specified.

The ring drive face 36 is a short plain face at the latch end of the ring, presented at the outer boundary of the annulus so that a wedge acting from outside the ring can bear on it; which segment carries it, and its position, form, extent and depth, are not specified and are shown schematically.

input.summary: Three findings, all confined to figure briefs, all fixed. The two FIG. 2 findings were cured by one edit: ring drive face 36 is now a short plain face at the latch end of the ring, against which the wedge bears, with the carrying segment and the position, form, extent and depth unspecified and shown schematically. That deletes the clause presenting the face at the outer boundary of the annulus with a wedge acting from outside the ring, so the brief no longer fixes a radial end position or a contact approach for a functional drive face, and it no longer locates the face in the same sentence that declares its position unspecified. The FIG. 2 leader for 36 was retargeted to the short plain face at the latch end of the ring, near the right joint, so the numeral list carries no outer-boundary placement either; the cam ring leader stays on the outer boundary in the upper left, clear of the drive face and of both joints. In FIG. 1 the latch lever now has its attitude shown schematically and is drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position, which keeps the over-center depiction that draft/07-drawings.md requires while dropping the assertion that leaning toward the first frame half is the over-center attitude. That gives FIG. 1 the same hedge FIG. 4 already carries for handle attitude, and the two briefs remain geometrically consistent, since up and to the right in FIG. 4's viewing sense is toward the first frame half. FIG. 4 was left as it stands, since its header already lists the position, form and extent of the ring drive face and its carrier, the extent of its contact with the wedge 52 and the wedge's direction of advance among the schematic items. No claim, no sentence of the detailed description, no drawing description, no Abstract text and no entry in draft/numerals.md changed; the description continues to say only that the ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge 52 can reach. Every numeral listed for each sheet is still named on it, and all six briefs are within the length limit, FIG. 1 at about 2488 characters and FIG. 2 at about 1987.
reasoning: The two FIG. 2 findings had one cause, so one edit closed both. Removing the outer-boundary clause takes out the untraced radial position and approach direction, and with it the contradiction between locating the face and calling its position unspecified. What remains is the one thing the disclosure supports, a face at the latch end that the wedge bears on.

The leader had to move with the sentence. Leaving the numeral list pointing at the outer boundary would have kept the deleted geometry alive in the part of the brief the renderer uses to place labels, so 36 now points at the same latch-end face the prose describes, identified by proximity to the right joint rather than by a radial position.

I left FIG. 4 untouched deliberately. Its housing, cavity and wedge are disclosed parts whose arrangement has been settled across earlier passes, and its header already marks the drive face's position, form and extent, its carrier, the extent of the wedge contact and the wedge's direction of advance as schematic, so nothing there asserts what FIG. 2 was asserting.

For FIG. 1 the fix is a hedge, not a deletion, because the drawing description requires that sheet to show the latch in the over-center position and a lever has to lean some way to be drawn. Marking the attitude schematic and saying the lean represents the over-center position keeps the required depiction while removing the claim that this particular lean is what over-center means.

No application text moved because none of it recites a radial position for the drive face, an approach direction for the wedge, or a handle lean. That neutrality in the claims, the summary and the description is what kept all three fixes inside figures/.

sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form and extent of the ring drive face 36 and its carrier; the extent of its contact with the wedge 52 and the wedge's direction of advance; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

One of the two bands presents the ring drive face 36 in its face, a short plain face; which segment carries it, and its position, form and extent, are not specified and are shown schematically.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the band circumferentially.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the frame body, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriage 30 with its follower 32, and the jaw pad 40 each carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block is received in the groove between its walls above and below, held against radial movement and free to move circumferentially, the fit shown schematically. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One rectangular opening is formed through that block, sized to receive the follower 32. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the opening beside the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel holding the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form and extent of the ring drive face 36; the extent of its contact with the wedge 52; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

The right band, the first cam ring segment 22, presents the ring drive face 36 in its face adjacent the parting line, a short plain face; its form and extent are not specified and are shown schematically.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance driving that band to the right, away from the parting line, so that the coupled ring is moved circumferentially in the direction that advances the jaw carriages inwardly.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the short plain face on the right band, the first cam ring segment 22, where the wedge 52 meets it.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

input.summary: Four findings, all fixed. Ring drive face 36 now has one carrier in both views: FIG. 2 gives it to the first cam ring segment 22 at that segment's latch end, on the upper side of the right joint, with form, extent and depth unspecified and schematic, and FIG. 4 gives it to the right band, the first cam ring segment 22, in its face adjacent the parting line, with form and extent unspecified and schematic. Both numeral entries were retargeted to that same face on segment 22, so numeral 36 can no longer land on different elements in the two sheets. In the Brief Description, FIG. 6 is now drawn with a portion of the frame broken away over the region shown, so the application text no longer states which axial side of the annular guide is closed; the FIG. 6 brief keeps that closure choice, where it is labelled schematic. FIG. 3's schematic list now also covers the way the radial guide 38 meets the mouth of the annular guide 18 and the position on the jaw carriage 30 from which the follower 32 projects together with its direction of projection, so those two forced depiction choices no longer read as asserted structure. The two drive directions are now coordinated so the rendered set matches the specification: FIG. 4 states that the wedge's advance drives the band carrying the face to the right, away from the parting line, moving the coupled ring in the direction that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, and the wedge's direction of advance was removed from that sheet's schematic list; FIG. 2 states that the end of each slot nearer the inner boundary lies clockwise, as seen in that view, of the end nearer the outer boundary, so the counter-clockwise ring rotation produced by the wedge's advance in FIG. 4 moves all three followers inwardly. I checked that pairing against the view handedness: FIG. 4 is the mirrored view, so driving segment 22 away from the latch-end parting line there is counter-clockwise as seen in FIG. 1 and FIG. 2, and a follower held at a fixed angular position by its radial guide then travels toward the inner end of its slot. In the FIG. 2 sentence I referred to the wedge in FIG. 4 without its numeral, since the wedge is not shown on that sheet and numeral 52 is not in its list. The claims, the detailed description, the Summary, the Abstract and draft/numerals.md are unchanged, and every brief remains within the length limit, the largest being FIG. 6 at about 2653 characters.
reasoning: The carrier of the drive face is a forced choice, not an invention assertion: the wedge has to bear on one face, so leaving it open in both briefs guaranteed that two independently rendered sheets would eventually disagree and put one numeral on two different parts. I made the choice once, on segment 22, and applied it to the prose and to both numeral targets so the leaders cannot drift apart from the text.

The FIG. 6 phrase in the Brief Description was the one place where a rendering convention had leaked into application text. Which axial side of the guide is closed is nowhere in the disclosure, and the FIG. 3 brief already calls the guide's opening direction schematic, so the neutral break-away phrasing puts the convention back where it belongs while leaving the figure briefs free to draw it.

For FIG. 3 the fix was a label, not a deletion, because a section through a carriage and a ring has to show some passage from the carriage to the slot. Naming the guide-to-guide meeting and the follower's origin and projection direction as schematic keeps the drawable geometry while making clear the disclosure fixes neither.

The direction coordination is the one place where two schematic hedges combined into a real risk: independently chosen, a slot tilt and a wedge advance can depict a mechanism that drives the jaws outward, contradicting claim 1. Pinning both in the briefs adds no structure, since inward travel is the disclosed function; it just stops the drawings from contradicting it.

I verified the direction pair rather than copying it. FIG. 4 is viewed from the side opposite FIG. 1, so pushing segment 22 rightward away from the parting line there maps to counter-clockwise in FIG. 1 and FIG. 2; with the follower angularly fixed by its radial guide, counter-clockwise ring motion carries it toward whichever slot end lies clockwise, which is why the inner end must be the clockwise one.

I kept the numeral out of the FIG. 2 cross-reference to the wedge. The sentence needs to name the member whose advance sets the rotation sense, but putting numeral 52 in a brief whose numeral list does not carry it is exactly the sort of mismatch the numeral check catches, and the cross-reference to FIG. 4 reads the same without it.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn fixed which segment the drawings put the drive face on, coordinated two drawn directions so the figures depict the inward travel the claims recite, labelled two FIG. 3 depiction choices as schematic, and made one Brief Description phrase neutral; the claims remain direction-neutral and segment-neutral, so claim scope is unchanged. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

The Brief Description now says FIG. 6 is viewed with a portion of the frame broken away over the region shown, so the application text no longer fixes which axial side of the annular guide is closed, while the FIG. 6 brief keeps that choice as a labelled convention. I confirmed that pairing against the mirrored view handedness rather than assuming it. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. # FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, and the positions and tilt of the three slots.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, the end of each slot nearer the inner boundary lying clockwise, as seen in this view, of the end nearer the outer boundary, so that the counter-clockwise rotation of the ring produced by advance of the wedge in FIG. 4 moves all three followers inwardly.

The ring drive face 36 is a short plain face carried by the first cam ring segment 22 at its latch end, on the upper side of the right joint; its form, extent and depth are not specified and are shown schematically.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form and extent of the ring drive face 36; the extent of its contact with the wedge 52; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

The right band, the first cam ring segment 22, presents the ring drive face 36 in its face adjacent the parting line, a short plain face; its form and extent are not specified and are shown schematically.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance driving that band to the right, away from the parting line, so that the coupled ring is moved circumferentially in the direction that advances the jaw carriages inwardly.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form and extent of the ring drive face 36; the extent of its contact with the wedge 52; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

One band presents the ring drive face 36, a short plain face where the wedge 52 meets it; the band that carries it, its position along that band, and its form and extent are not specified and are shown schematically.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance bearing on the ring drive face 36 so as to move the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, the direction of that movement in this view being unspecified and shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

input.summary: Five findings, all fixed, all in figure briefs. FIG. 2 no longer fixes the cam-slot handedness or the rotation sense: the three slots are alike and tilt the same way so that turning of the ring in one sense moves all three followers inwardly, with the handedness of the tilt and the corresponding sense of ring rotation unspecified and shown schematically. FIG. 4 no longer fixes the circumferential direction of the wedge drive: the wedge bears on the ring drive face 36 and its advance moves the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, with the direction of that movement in that view unspecified and shown schematically. The ring drive face is no longer assigned to a named segment or a named end position: FIG. 2 presents it as a short plain face of the segmented cam ring 20 at the latch end of the ring where the wedge reaches it, with its position along the ring, form, extent and depth unspecified and schematic, and FIG. 4 has one band present it as a short plain face where the wedge 52 meets it, with the carrying band, the position along that band, and the form and extent unspecified and schematic; both numeral targets were rewritten to match, so numeral 36 no longer points at a segment-specific location in either sheet. Those three edits also clear the fourth finding: with neither the drive direction nor the drive-face end position asserted, nothing in the brief set implies that the wedge works by separating the latch-end coupling faces, so FIG. 6 and the description remain the only account of the clamped state, in which the segments are coupled at both ends. FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 no longer state the assembly topology of the guide groove: in both, the groove is open on one side with the side on which it opens unspecified and schematic, and in FIG. 3 the follower post now extends from the jaw carriage 30 through the mouth of the groove into the slot opening with the position from which it projects and its direction of projection unspecified and schematic. Because the follower hedge now sits in the body text where the geometry is described, I removed the duplicate of it from the FIG. 3 header list, which also kept that brief within the length limit at about 2684 characters. I made two small tidies created by the replacements themselves: the FIG. 4 wedge sentence no longer names the drive face twice, and the FIG. 5 groove sentence no longer carries two schematic hedges for the same opening. The claims, detailed description, drawing description, Summary, Abstract and draft/numerals.md are unchanged, every numeral listed for a sheet is still named on it, and all six briefs are within the length limit.
reasoning: The slot handedness and the wedge drive direction had been pinned in an earlier pass to keep the two sheets from depicting a mechanism that drove the jaws outward. This review reads them as substantive cam geometry, so I removed both and relied instead on the functional statement each brief now carries: the slots tilt alike so that turning in one sense drives the followers inward, and the wedge's advance moves the ring in the sense that advances the carriages inwardly. The disclosed result is stated without naming a direction.

Withdrawing the segment attribution for the drive face was the edit that mattered most for internal consistency. Putting the face on the latch end of segment 22 and driving that segment away from the joint meant the wedge worked by parting the very coupling faces the description says stay coupled at both ends in the closed condition. Removing the location and the direction together removes that contradiction at its source rather than papering over it in FIG. 6.

I rewrote both numeral targets alongside the prose. A leader instruction that still pointed at a face on a named segment would have kept the withdrawn geometry alive in the part of the brief that places labels, which is how the same assertion has come back in earlier passes.

For the guide groove I kept a positive reason for the opening rather than only a hedge: the groove is open on one side so that the follower can reach the block in it. That gives the renderer something to draw and ties the opening to the disclosed engagement, while leaving which side is open unspecified.

Adding the follower hedge to the body text made the identical item in the FIG. 3 header redundant, and with both in place that brief would have run past the character limit. Removing the header duplicate was the way to satisfy the finding and the length gate with one change instead of trading one defect for another.

The two tidies were consequences of the suggested replacements meeting the existing sentences, not independent edits: the FIG. 4 wedge sentence would otherwise have said bears on the ring drive face twice in one clause, and the FIG. 5 groove sentence would have hedged the opening direction twice.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn withdrew drawing-level statements of slot handedness, rotation sense, wedge drive direction, drive-face carrier and position, and guide-groove assembly topology, none of which appears in any claim, so claim scope is unchanged and the claims remain direction-neutral and segment-neutral. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Ledger result: the substantive content of the application traces cleanly to the inventor's disclosure (which is textually identical to the single USER passage in input/conversation.md). Every limitation of claims 1-15, every one of the 26 reference numerals, and the technical statements in the Field, Summary, Detailed Description and Abstract map to affirmative source wording: split frame of two semicircular halves with hinge at one end and releasable latch at the other; three radial jaw carriages in radial guides with pivoting concave jaw pads and no tool-specific pipe diameter; segmented cam ring retained in an annular guide with one segment per half; complementary faces at the hinge and latch ends coupling the segments on closure; followers in oblique slots converting a limited ring rotation into synchronized inward travel; a wedge driven by the latch against a drive face of the ring; the first (holding) and second (over-center) latch positions; the force-limiting spring stack between handle and wedge absorbing remaining travel; the indicator pin read against a fixed edge of the latch housing over a predetermined compression range and expressly not a diameter measurement; carriage return springs; the install/remove method; and the optional mounting boss outside the annular guide carrying a sensor, tool or conduit and not participating in synchronization. The Background is prior-art characterization and is exempt here; the title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md (no priority claim, no federally sponsored research). # FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, and the positions and tilt of the three slots.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, so that turning of the ring in one sense moves all three followers inwardly; the handedness of the tilt, and the corresponding sense of ring rotation, are not specified and are shown schematically.

The ring drive face 36 is a short plain face presented by the segmented cam ring 20 at the latch end of the ring, where the wedge reaches it; its position along the ring, form, extent and depth are not specified and are shown schematically.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper left.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the short plain face on the segmented cam ring 20 at the latch end where the wedge acts.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position, form and extent of the ring drive face 36; the extent of its contact with the wedge 52; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

One band presents the ring drive face 36, a short plain face where the wedge 52 meets it; the band that carries it, its position along that band, and its form and extent are not specified and are shown schematically.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance moving the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, the direction of that movement in this view being unspecified and shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall and leaning past upright, the over-center position. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, and the positions and tilt of the three slots.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way, so that turning of the ring in one sense moves all three followers inwardly; the handedness of the tilt, and the corresponding sense of ring rotation, are not specified and are shown schematically.

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper left.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.

input.summary: Three findings, all in figure briefs, all fixed. FIG. 4 no longer verbalizes the form or extent of ring drive face 36: one band presents the face at the place where the wedge 52 meets it, and the band that carries it, its position along that band, and the form, extent and contact geometry of the face are stated to be undisclosed and to carry no technical assertion, with only a bare generic face drawn at the point of contact. The self-contradiction is gone with the words that caused it, and the schematic list item now reads as the position of the ring drive face 36 and the place at which the wedge 52 bears on it, together with the extent of that contact. I also retargeted the FIG. 4 leader for 36, which still carried the short plain face wording, so it now points at the face on the band where the wedge 52 bears on it; leaving that phrase in the numeral list would have reinstated the same form and extent assertion in the part of the brief that places labels. FIG. 4 no longer equates a handle angle with the over-center condition: the latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width rising up and to the right from the top wall, its attitude shown schematically and drawn only to represent the latch in the over-center position, asserting no particular angle or over-center geometry, with its mounting still not depicted. That matches how FIG. 1 already treats the lever. FIG. 2 no longer asserts that the ring face carries nothing but the slots: the region within the inner boundary is open, the three slots open between the two boundaries, and features of the ring other than the two joints and the three slots are not designated in that view, which also removes the tension with the ring drive face 36 that the description recites as a further feature of the same segmented cam ring 20 and that FIG. 4 alone now labels. The claims, detailed description, drawing description, Summary, Abstract and draft/numerals.md are unchanged; numeral 36 remains defined once in the table, used in the description, and shown on FIG. 4. All six briefs are within the length limit, the largest being FIG. 3 at about 2684 characters and FIG. 4 at about 2655.
reasoning: The drive-face wording had been carrying two words that do real technical work. Plain says the face is not a ramp and short says how far it runs, which is exactly the kind of statement a later reader would take as the shape of a cam surface. Replacing them with an instruction to draw a bare generic face at the point of contact keeps the sheet renderable and leaves the geometry where the disclosure left it.

I extended the fix to the numeral entry even though the finding cited the prose. The leader instruction repeated short plain face verbatim, and in earlier passes the numeral list is precisely where withdrawn geometry has survived and come back, so the target now identifies the face by its contact with the wedge rather than by form.

For the handle the fix is a hedge rather than a deletion, because FIG. 4 has to show the latch in the over-center position and a bar has to be drawn at some angle. Saying the attitude represents that position and asserts no over-center geometry gives the renderer what it needs without making the drawn angle definitional, and it brings FIG. 4 in line with the wording FIG. 1 already uses.

The FIG. 2 sentence was a negative assertion doing no drawing work: the renderer only needs to know to draw a plain annulus with the three slots opening in it, not that nothing else exists on the ring. Replacing it with a statement that other features are simply not designated in that view also resolves the awkwardness of a sheet denying features while the description recites a further feature of the same ring.

No application text moved, and none should have: the description already says only that the ring drive face is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge can reach, and the claims recite an over-center position without an angle. Those neutral statements are what allowed all three fixes to stay inside figures/, and they remain the authority the drawings follow.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn withdrew drawing-level statements about the form and extent of the drive face, a handle angle, and the absence of other features on the ring surface, none of which appears in any claim, so claim scope is unchanged. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	SCOPE. Technical authority: input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (identical text). input/brief.md was used only for the title, applicant/inventor, no-priority and no-government-support formalities. review/previous-qa.md and input/request.md are context only; the request's instruction to "continue automatic filing repair" affirms no technical content. No rendered images were inspected.
4	
5	LEDGER - CLAIMS. Every limitation of claims 1-15 traces to an affirmative inventor passage. Claim 1: split first/second frame halves "joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end"; annular guide and three radial guides from "Three radial jaw carriages... Each carriage slides in a radial guide" and "retained in an annular guide of the frame"; "a pivoting concave jaw pad"; "One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half"; "complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring"; "a follower received in a respective oblique slot"; "The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages"; "Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring"; "A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others"; "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released". Claims 2-3 trace to "A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range... does not measure pipe diameter". Claim 4 to the disclosed first/second over-center positions. Claim 5 to "bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter". Claims 6-7 to retention of one segment per half plus the coupling being made and broken by closing/opening. Claims 8 and 10 to "The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization." Claim 9 to "semicircular frame half" and "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame". Claims 13-15 to the disclosed install/remove sequence.
