# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the frame body, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriage 30 with its follower 32, and the jaw pad 40 each carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, the way the radial guide 38 meets the mouth of the annular guide 18, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, open on one side so that the follower 32 can reach the block in it, the side on which it opens and its proportions being unspecified and shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block is received in the groove between its walls above and below, held against radial movement and free to move circumferentially, the fit shown schematically. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One rectangular opening is formed through that block, sized to receive the follower 32. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends from the jaw carriage 30 through the mouth of the groove and into that opening, the position from which it projects and its direction of projection being unspecified and shown schematically, its sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

input.summary: One finding, confined to two figure briefs, and it is fixed. FIG. 3 no longer declares the opening side of annular guide 18 unspecified while its own layout determines it: the groove now opens toward the side of the view on which the channel lies, so that the follower 32 can pass from the channel into the groove, with that choice and the groove's proportions stated as a drawing convention shown schematically. FIG. 5 now pins the axial sense of its view, saying the view's right is the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed, as in FIG. 3, and its groove is drawn opening toward the same side of the view as the groove in FIG. 3, again as a drawing convention shown schematically. The same numbered part is therefore drawn the same way in both views the description tells the reader to compare, and the choice remains consistent with FIG. 6, which breaks away the near wall on the FIG. 1 side to expose the cam ring segments. While making that harmonization I removed one statement in FIG. 3 that the same reasoning had just made untenable: the follower post was said to project in an unspecified direction, although a post that reaches the slot through the groove mouth necessarily projects toward the groove. The brief now marks only the position on the carriage from which the post projects as a drawing convention, which keeps the undisclosed detail hedged without leaving a hedge the surrounding geometry contradicts. I also shortened the hatching sentence in the FIG. 3 header, since the added wording had brought that brief close to the character limit; it now sits at about 2694 characters, with FIG. 5 at about 1957 and every other brief unchanged and within the limit. No application text changed: the claims, detailed description, drawing description, Summary, Abstract and draft/numerals.md stay silent about the axial arrangement, every numeral listed for a sheet is still named on it, and numeral 18 continues to denote one part in the table, the description, FIG. 3, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6.
reasoning: The defect was a hedge that had outlived its geometry. FIG. 3 already placed the groove on one side of the body and the channel on the other, with the follower crossing between them, so calling the opening side unspecified told the renderer something the rest of the brief contradicted. Naming the side by reference to the channel keeps the instruction internally consistent and still marks it as a convention rather than disclosed structure.

FIG. 5 needed two things, not one: a rule tying its groove to FIG. 3's, and an axial reference frame in which that rule means something. Without stating that its right is the FIG. 1 side, an instruction to open toward the same side as FIG. 3 would have been unresolvable, so both were added.

I checked the choice against FIG. 6 rather than assuming it. FIG. 6 is viewed from the FIG. 1 side and breaks away the wall nearest that viewer, which only exposes the segments if the guide is closed on that side and opens away from it, which is exactly what the FIG. 3 layout gives.

The follower projection hedge had to go for the same reason the guide hedge did. Once the groove opens toward the channel, a post passing through the mouth into the slot can only project toward the groove, so leaving its direction declared unspecified would have recreated the defect one paragraph later. The position on the carriage is still undisclosed and is still hedged.

The added wording pushed FIG. 3 toward the length gate, so I paid for it inside the same file by compressing the hatching sentence, which keeps the requirement that each cut element differ from its neighbours while dropping words that carried no geometry.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn harmonized a depiction convention about which axial side the annular guide opens on, which no claim recites and which the description leaves silent, so claim scope is unchanged. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

The Summary now reads that one latch motion, applied at one point on the cam ring, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the Detailed Description now reads that one input, applied at one point on the cam ring, reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element. Both previously located that input on one frame half, which the disclosure never does: it says only that closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring, and the wedge acts at the latch end, where both segments and both halves meet, so a drive face at or spanning that joint is equally within the disclosure. The filed text now matches what FIG. 4 already says, that the band carrying the ring drive face is not disclosed and carries no technical assertion. Nothing else needed changing: the sentences keep the supported point in full, that a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring so a single input reaches all three carriages through one element, with the relationship between the carriages set by the geometry of the ring rather than by how the clamp is operated. I searched the rest of draft/ and figures/ for any other localization of the drive input to a half and found none, so the claims, the Abstract, the drawing description, the numeral table and all six figure briefs are unchanged and remain synchronized. Claim scope is untouched, since no claim ever recited where on the frame the input enters; claim 1 recites only a wedge movable by the latch and positioned to bear on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring.
reasoning: The assertion was doing rhetorical work rather than technical work. The point those two paragraphs exist to make is that splitting the clamp does not split the drive, because the coupled ring carries one input to all three carriages. Naming a frame half as the entry point added a fact the inventor never supplied without strengthening that argument, so removing it costs the specification nothing.

I used the cam ring as the neutral referent rather than the latch end or the joint, because the disclosure does say the wedge bears on a drive face of the cam ring. That keeps the sentence anchored to disclosed structure instead of trading one unsupported location for another.

The internal disagreement mattered as much as the source gap: FIG. 4 expressly refuses to say which band carries the drive face, so the text was asserting exactly what the drawing declined to assert. The two now agree, and the description remains silent about which segment or half receives the input.

I checked the rest of the application for the same localization before returning, since this phrasing had appeared in two separate sections and could plausibly have been echoed in the Background or the Abstract. It is not, so the fix is complete at two sentences.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the frame body, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriage 30 with its follower 32, and the jaw pad 40 each at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, the way the radial guide 38 meets the mouth of the annular guide 18, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, the groove opening toward the side of the view on which the channel lies, so that the follower 32 can pass from the channel into the groove, that choice and the groove's proportions being a drawing convention shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block is received in the groove between its walls above and below, held against radial movement and free to move circumferentially, the fit shown schematically. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One rectangular opening is formed through that block, sized to receive the follower 32. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends from the jaw carriage 30 through the mouth of the groove and into that opening, the position on the carriage from which it projects being a drawing convention shown schematically, its sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position of the ring drive face 36 and the place at which the wedge 52 bears on it; the extent of that contact; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

One band presents the ring drive face 36 at the place where the wedge 52 meets it. The band that carries it, its position along that band, and the form, extent and contact geometry of the face are not disclosed and are to carry no technical assertion; draw only a bare generic face at the point of contact.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance moving the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, the direction of that movement in this view being unspecified and shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall, its attitude shown schematically and drawn only to represent the latch in the over-center position, asserting no particular angle or over-center geometry. Its mounting is not depicted.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the position of the ring drive face 36 and the place at which the wedge 52 bears on it; the extent of that contact; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces, and the channel holding each band opens at that body's end face.

One band presents the ring drive face 36 at the place where the wedge 52 meets it. The band that carries it, its position along that band, and the form, extent and contact geometry of the face are not disclosed and are to carry no technical assertion; draw only a bare generic face at the point of contact.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance moving the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, the direction of that movement in this view being unspecified and shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

Its lower end meets the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58, so that the bar is not drawn as a detached element; no pivot, mounting detail, angle or over-center geometry is depicted there.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

input.summary: Three findings, all in figure briefs, all fixed. FIG. 3 no longer verbalizes the architecture of the two guides: the body is now simply formed with a groove and with a channel, the groove is bounded on its radially outer side above and its radially inner side below with its proportions a drawing convention shown schematically, the channel opens at the underside of the body radially inward, and the follower post extends from the jaw carriage 30 into the slot opening without passing through any stated groove mouth. The schematic list drops the guide opening direction and the guide-to-guide junction, leaving the carriage return spring 44 and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20. FIG. 5 matches: its groove is bounded on its radially outer side above and its radially inner side below, with the opening-side sentence removed. FIG. 3 no longer names a spring type: a spring, drawn as a zigzag spring symbol, acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage radially outward, and I retargeted the numeral 44 leader to the zigzag spring symbol so the list matches the prose. FIG. 4 no longer leaves the latch handle floating: its lower end meets the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58 so the bar is not drawn as a detached element, with no pivot, mounting detail, angle or over-center geometry depicted there. That addition pushed the FIG. 4 brief over the character limit, so I trimmed the same file: the schematic list no longer repeats the drive-face position, contact place and contact extent, which the body paragraph already de-asserts more strongly by stating that the carrying band, the position along it, and the form, extent and contact geometry are not disclosed and carry no technical assertion; and the sentence about each band's channel opening at its body's end face is gone, which also removes a guide-opening statement of the same kind the first finding targets. FIG. 4 now measures about 2668 characters and FIG. 3 about 2372, with every other brief unchanged and within the limit. The claims, detailed description, drawing description, Summary, Abstract and draft/numerals.md are unchanged, and every numeral listed for a sheet is still named on it.
reasoning: The guide architecture was the substantive item, and the honest repair was subtraction rather than rewording. Each sheet still shows a groove holding the ring, a channel holding the carriage, and a post reaching the slot, which is all the disclosure supplies; what came out was the axial side the groove opens toward and the statement that the channel runs from that opening, since the source never places the ring axially beside the carriage or joins the two guides.

Removing the opening direction from FIG. 3 forced the matching removal in FIG. 5. Those two sheets section the same guide in the same orientation, so leaving the harmonization sentence in FIG. 5 would have pointed at a choice FIG. 3 no longer makes.

The spring type was a one-word structural assertion that the zigzag symbol does not need. Calling it a spring drawn as a spring symbol keeps the drawing identical while leaving open whether the bias is produced in compression or tension, which the inventor did not say. I moved the leader target to the same words so the numeral list cannot reintroduce the type.

For the handle I made the bar meet the housing rather than adding any joint. Both the handle and the housing are disclosed parts of the latch, and the description already places the spring stack in a drive train between handle and wedge, so a bar floating clear of everything was a drawing defect against text that was already correct. The added clause is explicit that no pivot, angle or over-center geometry is depicted at that meeting.

The two trims in FIG. 4 were chosen so they did no damage: the schematic list item was strictly weaker than the body sentence that replaced it, and the clause about each channel opening at its body's end face was the same class of guide-opening assertion this review asked me to remove from FIG. 3, so dropping it served both the finding and the length gate.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn removed drawing-level statements about guide opening direction and guide-to-guide junction, a spring type, and a detached handle depiction, none of which appears in any claim, so claim scope is unchanged. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces.

One band presents the ring drive face 36 at the place where the wedge 52 meets it. The band that carries it, its position along that band, and the form, extent and contact geometry of the face are not disclosed and are to carry no technical assertion; draw only a bare generic face at the point of contact.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance moving the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, the direction of that movement in this view being unspecified and shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall, its attitude shown schematically and drawn only to represent the latch in the over-center position, asserting no particular angle or over-center geometry. Its lower end meets the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58, so that the bar is not drawn as a detached element; no pivot, mounting detail, angle or over-center geometry is depicted there.

Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. Cut material carries section hatching; the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each cam ring segment at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches, so the parting line and the segment end contact stay distinct. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, filling the upper and lower parts of the view, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge, and the wall of the channel on that side, its radially inner side, faces the block lying in the channel. input.summary: I ran the checks the request asks for against the current application and left the filing text untouched, because nothing in it is defective. Both mechanical failures have a single cause: the sheets for FIG. 3, FIG. 4, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 have not been rendered. All six brief files are present in figures/ and each is complete, so the drawing plan itself is sound. I verified numeral coverage sheet by sheet: FIG. 1 carries 100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 30, 40 and 90; FIG. 2 carries 20, 22, 24, 26, 28 and 34; FIG. 3 carries 18, 20, 30, 32, 34, 38, 40 and 44; FIG. 4 carries 22, 24, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56 and 58; FIG. 5 carries 18, 20, 70 and 80; FIG. 6 carries 10, 12, 18, 22, 24 and 28. That union is all 26 numerals in draft/numerals.md, and the twelve reported as absent, 18, 32, 36, 38, 44, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58, 70 and 80, are exactly the numerals that live only on the four unrendered sheets. So the coverage failure is a symptom of the missing sheets, and I removed no part, numeral definition, or supporting text to silence it. Every numeral listed on a sheet is also named in that sheet's prose, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, the Brief Description lists exactly the six figures the briefs describe, and the detailed description calls out each of FIG. 1 through FIG. 6. Section designation 3-3 remains identical in the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 3 brief, draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md. Each brief is within the character limit, the longest bodies being about 2668 for FIG. 4 and about 2653 for FIG. 6. To reduce the chance that a regeneration stalls or renders ambiguously, I made two small hardening edits in the affected briefs and nothing else. In FIG. 4, the sentence fixing the latch handle to the housing now states the contact positively, that its lower end meets the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58 so the bar stands on the housing, the meeting drawn as a plain contact, instead of listing what is not depicted there; the same paragraph already marks the handle's attitude schematic and disclaims any particular angle or over-center geometry, so nothing is asserted that was not asserted before. In FIG. 3, the radial guide leader now targets a side wall of the channel holding the jaw carriage 30 rather than the right wall, since the earlier fix removed the statement placing the groove and channel on particular sides of that view and left the ordinal without a fixed referent. The remaining step is mechanical and belongs to the image pipeline: regenerate the four missing sheets from the existing briefs and re-run the numeral, leader, OCR and geometry checks. No claim, description, drawing description, Abstract or numeral-table text changed this turn.
reasoning: Before touching anything I checked whether the coverage failure indicated a real plan defect. It does not: the twelve missing numerals map exactly onto FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, and the numerals shared with FIG. 1 or FIG. 2 were not reported. That pattern only occurs when those sheets exist as specifications but not as images, so redistributing labels or adding a sheet would have damaged a correct plan.

I deliberately did not move any numeral onto FIG. 1 or FIG. 2 to make the check pass. Those two views cannot show a sectioned guide, a follower in its slot, the latch drive train or the mounting boss, and forcing their numerals onto a plan view would have produced leaders pointing at nothing and broken the rule that each numeral denotes one part in every view.

The FIG. 4 handle sentence was worth rewording on its own terms. It had been phrased as a list of things not depicted, which is the kind of negative control that gives a renderer nothing positive to draw; stating the contact affirmatively keeps the handle attached, which was the point of the earlier fix, without relying on a prohibition.

The FIG. 3 leader fix repairs a loose end left by the previous pass. When the groove-and-channel side placement came out of that brief, the phrase the right wall lost its anchor, so the target now names a side wall generically, which still distinguishes the guide surface from the carriage body it holds.

I left the application text alone because the review raised nothing against it and my own pass found nothing: numerals are one-to-one, the section designation matches in all four required places, the Brief Description and the detailed description agree with the six briefs, and no placeholder or drafting note is present.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn changed only two drawing-level details and no claim language, so claim scope is unchanged. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.

The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces.

One band presents the ring drive face 36 at the place where the wedge 52 meets it. The band that carries it, its position along that band, and the form, extent and contact geometry of the face are not disclosed and are to carry no technical assertion; draw only a bare generic face at the point of contact.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its walls enclosing a cavity that is open toward the band carrying the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity and bears on the ring drive face 36, its advance moving the coupled ring circumferentially in the sense that advances the jaw carriages inwardly, the direction of that movement in this view being unspecified and shown schematically.

In the cavity a zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 toward the latch handle 50. That line is the force-limiting spring stack 54, lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 stands above the latch housing 58 as a plain straight bar of even width, rising up and to the right from the top wall, its attitude shown schematically and drawn only to represent the latch in the over-center position, asserting no particular angle or over-center geometry. Its lower end meets the outer surface of the top wall of the latch housing 58, so the bar stands on the housing, the meeting being drawn as a plain contact.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects beyond the outer surface of the top wall, that surface being the fixed edge against which the pin is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the face on the band where the wedge 52 bears on it.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with a lever reaching radially outward from it, the lever's attitude shown schematically, drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, the topmost on the first frame half 10 and the others on the second frame half 12, these three circumferential positions and their distribution between the two frame halves being shown schematically. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the jaw carriage 30 is shown schematically as a block reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is a section designation rather than a reference numeral, and no leader line runs to it.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the topmost carriage block.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown, the frame and the two cam ring segments being shown in section at the break. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. Cut material carries section hatching; the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each cam ring segment at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches, so the parting line and the segment end contact stay distinct. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at each body's radially outer side.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, filling the upper and lower parts of the view, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge, and the wall of the channel on that side, its radially inner side, faces the block lying in the channel. The irregular break line of each body runs along the radially outer boundary of its channel, so the view shows nothing of what lies radially outward of the two blocks at this joint.

A solid block lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the end faces of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another where they meet, so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other; the form of those surfaces and the extent of their engagement are shown schematically. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target well inside the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the channel wall in the upper body on the radially inner side of the block that lies in the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body at a slant different from that of every other cut element beside it; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the attitude and outline of the latch handle 50; and the drawn path of the force-limiting spring stack 54, shown as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces.

One band presents the ring drive face 36 at the place where the wedge 52 meets it. input.summary: The three reviewer findings are fixed in the briefs. FIG. 4 now shows the drive train unbroken: the zigzag line runs upward from the wedge 52 to the lower end of the latch handle 50, and the handle's lower end passes through an opening in the top wall of the latch housing 58 to meet the upper end of the force-limiting spring stack 54, so the bar is continuous with the drive train, with the form of that meeting shown schematically and asserting no pivot or mounting detail. That makes the sheet show what the Brief Description says it shows, the drive train between the latch handle and the segmented cam ring, and it matches the description's statement that the spring stack lies in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The naming inconsistency in FIG. 1 is gone: the element formerly called a lever is now described as a straight bar of the latch 16 reaching radially outward from the schematic latch block, its attitude shown schematically and drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position, so no second name for the latch handle survives anywhere in the briefs. I did not add numeral 50 to the FIG. 1 list, because that sheet already carries eight numerals, which is the per-sheet ceiling, and numeral 50 already has its home on FIG. 4; describing the bar generically as part of the numbered latch 16 removes the competing name without overcrowding the sheet or touching any specification text. The generic-word collision is also gone: the annular guide 18 is a groove in FIG. 3, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 alike, and channel now names only the radial guide 38 in FIG. 3, with the FIG. 6 numeral entries for 10, 12 and 18 updated to the same word. Adding the drive-train continuity took FIG. 4 past the character limit, so I trimmed the same brief where it had become repetitive: the meeting hedge no longer repeats the angle and over-center carve-out that the preceding sentence already makes, and the wedge sentence states that the direction of ring movement in that view is unspecified without also labelling it schematic. FIG. 4 now measures about 2744 characters, FIG. 1 about 2578 and FIG. 6 about 2642, all within the limit. The three mechanical checks remain rendering-stage: figures/ still holds only the six briefs, so FIG. 3 through FIG. 6 register as missing sheets, the FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 pixel consensus has no pixels to read, and the twelve listed numerals register as absent because they appear only on unrendered sheets. Sheet by sheet the briefs place all 26 numerals of draft/numerals.md, so no numeral was moved or removed and no application text changed this turn.
reasoning: The FIG. 4 defect was real and worth fixing exactly as identified: a sectioned, hatched wall drawn between the handle and the spring stack shows the handle outside the drive train, which is the one relationship the Brief Description promises that figure shows. The continuity is disclosed, since the inventor says the spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so drawing it costs nothing in fidelity.

On the FIG. 1 naming I fixed the defect the finding names, one element with two names, but not by adding a ninth numeral to that sheet. The eight-numeral ceiling exists so leaders stay readable, numeral 50 is already carried by FIG. 4, and the alternative of freeing a slot would have meant stripping a numeral such as the jaw pad from a sheet the detailed description ties it to. Describing the bar as part of the numbered latch 16 removes the second name outright.

The groove and channel collision was worth taking seriously because both words name real, separately numbered guides. Standardising on groove for the annular guide across the three briefs that show it, and reserving channel for the radial guide in the one brief that shows it, leaves no word mapping onto two parts.

The trims in FIG. 4 came out of the same paragraphs the additions went into, and only where the text had begun repeating its own hedges: the handle sentence already says the attitude is schematic and asserts no angle or over-center geometry, so the following clause did not need to say it again.

I again left the specification and the numeral assignments alone. The reviewer verified that the briefs place every specification numeral on a sheet and that the failures follow from sheets never having been rendered, so the corrective work here is confined to the briefs, and I created no image file since figure files in this workspace are Markdown specifications only.

The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The Background states the technical problems that combination addresses before they are needed in argument: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. This turn changed only figure-brief wording, so claim scope is unchanged. # FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with a straight bar of the latch 16 reaching radially outward from that block, the bar's attitude shown schematically, drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, the topmost on the first frame half 10 and the others on the second frame half 12, these three circumferential positions and their distribution between the two frame halves being shown schematically. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the jaw carriage 30 is shown schematically as a block reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is a section designation rather than a reference numeral, and no leader line runs to it.

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. If the gripping surfaces of each part are driven separately, the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive is given up: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. If the split body is instead pulled closed on the pipe, the closing force passes through the joint at the split and the pipe itself reacts the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe, and a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is needed, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. An added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

content.content: 5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the blocks that carry them.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with the latch handle 50 reaching radially outward from that block as a straight bar, the handle's attitude shown schematically, drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position.

Three blocks are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, one on the first frame half 10 and two on the second frame half 12, these three circumferential positions and their distribution between the two frame halves being shown schematically. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the block is shown schematically as reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each block carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost block, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is a section designation rather than a reference numeral, and no leader line runs to it.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the inner end of the topmost block.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar reaching radially outward from the latch block.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

input.summary: Both findings are fixed. In figures/FIG-1.md the element at the right joint is now the latch handle 50, reaching radially outward from the schematic latch block as a straight bar, with the handle's attitude shown schematically and drawn inclined toward the first frame half 10 to represent the latch in the over-center position, and numeral 50 was added to that sheet's list with a target well inside the straight bar reaching radially outward from the latch block. The element now carries one name and one numeral everywhere it appears, matching draft/numerals.md, the detailed description and the FIG. 4 brief. Adding 50 would have made nine numerals on that sheet, above the eight-per-sheet ceiling, so I moved jaw carriage 30 to the focused view that already carries it, FIG. 3, which is the sectional view of one jaw carriage with its follower, radial guide and return spring. Following the numeral-moving procedure, every use of that numeral and its canonical part name is gone from the FIG. 1 brief: the three carriages are now described there as three blocks spaced around the annular frame body, one on the first frame half 10 and two on the second frame half 12, each reaching radially inward through an opening in the inner circle, and the cutting-plane line now lies on the radial centre line of the topmost block. That required no change to the specification, because the detailed description ties FIG. 1 to the clamp 100, the pipe 90, the jaw pads 40, the two halves, the hinge 14 and the latch 16, and discusses the jaw carriages 30 without saying they are shown in FIG. 1, while expressly referring the carriage detail to FIG. 3. FIG. 1 now lists 100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 40, 50 and 90, which is eight, and the six sheets together still place all 26 numerals: 30 is carried by FIG. 3, and nothing was deleted or left without a home. In draft/05-background.md the closing paragraph now reads that it would be desirable to provide a split clamp in which the drive is coupled by the act of closing, every gripping element is advanced from that one drive, and the remaining lever travel is absorbed within the clamp and reported as a loading condition rather than a dimension, replacing the assertion about what has been lacking. The need is stated in the same terms without a factual claim about the field that no reference in prior_art/ supports. The three mechanical checks remain rendering-stage: figures/ still holds only the six briefs, so FIG. 3 through FIG. 6 register as missing sheets, the FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 semantic consensus has no pixels to read, and the twelve listed numerals register as absent because they appear only on unrendered sheets. All briefs stay within the character limit, the largest being FIG. 6 at about 2642 characters and FIG. 4 at about 2744.
reasoning: The naming defect was real and had survived a previous pass in a different form, so I gave the element its canonical name and numeral rather than reaching for another generic word. Calling it the latch handle 50 in FIG. 1 costs nothing in fidelity, since the handle is disclosed and the brief still marks its attitude as schematic.

That fix collided with the eight-numeral ceiling, and I resolved the collision by moving a numeral out rather than by crowding the sheet or inventing a seventh figure. Jaw carriage 30 was the right one to move: FIG. 3 is the focused sectional view of exactly that part and already carries it, so coverage is untouched.

I checked the description before moving it, because moving a numeral off a sheet is only safe if no text says that part is visible there. The FIG. 1 paragraph names the clamp, the pipe, the pads, the halves, the hinge and the latch, and the carriage paragraph carries no figure reference and already points the carriage detail to FIG. 3, so no specification sentence had to be edited to keep text and figures in step.

Having removed the numeral, I removed the canonical name with it and described the carriages as plain blocks, which is what the procedure requires when a sheet still needs the structure only as context. The pads remain numbered on FIG. 1 because the description says they are seated on the pipe in that view.

On the Background, the substance of the paragraph is the need the invention answers, not a survey of what exists, so restating it as a desideratum keeps the entire technical argument intact while removing the one sentence that asserted a fact about the field with no reference behind it. The earlier paragraphs already read as mechanical reasoning about split clamps rather than as claims about identified art.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background carries no citations and none was added. With no art of record, the Background now states the problems and the need in its own terms rather than asserting what the field lacks: dividing the drive element with the body surrenders the fixed relationship between the two sides so the clamp settles off center, a split body pulled closed on the pipe needs a part dimensioned to a particular diameter, and a rigid handle drive train forces residual travel into whichever pad touched first while an instrument reading jaw position reports pipe size rather than grip force. The independent claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the relationship the inventor calls essential: closing the frame halves is itself what couples the two cam ring segments into one ring through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, a wedge moved by the latch bears on a ring drive face and turns that coupled ring through a stroke, three oblique slots convert the rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, and a force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. That explanation sits in the specification ahead of any argument that may need it. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art available here may be incomplete and a later search could surface references bearing on these claims.
